Keep the Lineages Alive: Diversity-Preserving SMC for Diffusion LLM Decoding

Minoo Ahmadi    Seyedarmin Azizi    Mehdi Kamal    Massoud Pedram Affiliation: University of Southern California, Los Angeles, USA Affiliation: {minooahm, seyedarm, mehdi.kamal, pedram}@usc.edu
Abstract

Inference-time sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) decoding can improve the reasoning accuracy of masked diffusion language models (diffusion LLMs) without post-training by resampling a population of partial generations according to a reward. Its effectiveness therefore depends on the resampling step, which must concentrate computation on promising candidates while retaining enough diversity to explore alternative reasoning paths. The reward can be internal, the decoder’s own confidence on the committed prefix, or external, a process reward model scoring that prefix. Under either reward, multinomial resampling can disrupt this balance by duplicating high-weight particles and discarding lineages that may still reach a correct solution. The effective sample size (ESS) does not register this loss: multinomial resampling resets it to its maximum even as distinct lineages disappear. To retain such lineages, we introduce lineage-preserving SMC (LP-SMC), which combines Chopthin resampling with an input weight floor. Instead of equalizing weights, Chopthin bounds the ratio between the largest and smallest weights it returns and carries the unequal weights forward. The floor limits how far below the maximum a weight may fall before resampling, so that lineages with low early weight keep a chance to recover. Across mathematical-reasoning and code-generation benchmarks on two base models, LP-SMC raises oracle coverage, the fraction of problems with at least one correct particle, in every setting, by 1.81.8 to 25.625.6 points, and raises end-to-end accuracy under a common reward-model selector in eleven of twelve settings, by up to 7.97.9 points on LLaDA-1.5 and 18.318.3 on Dream-7B. The coverage gain persists under the external reward model, which suggests that diversity-preserving resampling and the guidance signal contribute separately to inference-time search.

1 Introduction

Inference-time scaling can improve language-model reasoning by allocating more computation during decoding (Brown et al., 2024; Snell et al., 2024), and sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) provides a probabilistic framework for it (Doucet et al., 2001), applied to autoregressive language models with learned twist functions or process rewards (Zhao et al., 2024; Puri et al., 2025) and to text diffusion models (Singhal et al., 2025). In particular, self-rewarding SMC (SR-SMC; Luo et al., 2026) weights each particle by the confidence accumulated along its own trajectory and improves diffusion LLMs on mathematical reasoning and code generation without further training.

Information can be lost during resampling itself. Recent SMC decoding methods introduce new proposal or weighting mechanisms while retaining standard resampling schemes; SR-SMC uses multinomial resampling, which converts continuous weights into a discrete number of descendants (Douc et al., 2005), replicating high-weight particles and discarding low-weight ones. In reasoning tasks a lineage that carries low intermediate weight may still develop into a correct completion, so resampling removes trajectories whose weight is currently low, not necessarily those that will ultimately be incorrect. Figure 1 illustrates this for a four-particle population, where the highest-weight lineage (the particles descending from one initial particle) is incorrect while a lower-weight correct lineage is removed. Declining to resample avoids the loss but forfeits the concentration of computation that motivates SMC; the question is how to resample without discarding what the population has already reached.

A better reward does not resolve this: improving the reward changes the weights, not the rule that converts them into descendants: a stronger process reward model still leaves multinomial resampling to discards the low-weight particles. Nor does the standard diagnostic, the effective sample size (ESS), measure this loss. Repeated resampling is known to reduce path diversity (Kitagawa, 1996; Doucet et al., 2001), yet the ESS measures weight imbalance, not how many lineages remain, and multinomial resampling resets it to its maximum while lineages disappear. We formalize this mismatch and show that multinomial resampling of equally weighted particles from distinct lineages eliminates roughly one third of them in expectation.

Preserving lineage diversity requires addressing two failure modes. First, a moderately weighted lineage may disappear solely through the stochasticity of resampling. Second, a lineage’s weight may fall so far below the maximum before resampling that it is unlikely to survive even under a diversity-preserving rule, which is common in block-wise decoding because the weight is a product over many committed tokens (Section 2.2). We address the first with Chopthin resampling (Gandy & Lau, 2016), which bounds the ratio between the returned weights instead of equalizing them and carries the unequal weights forward, and the second with a weight floor that limits how far below the maximum any weight may fall before resampling. Neither requires additional model evaluations. Together they form lineage-preserving SMC (LP-SMC); Section 4 derives the resulting ESS guarantee, the gate condition on the floor and the bias it introduces.

We keep the proposal fixed and evaluate population management under two forms of guidance, the internal self-reward of SR-SMC and an external process reward model, and under several selection rules, because constructing a population that contains a correct answer and selecting it are different problems. Across twelve model–guidance–benchmark settings, LP-SMC increases oracle coverage, the fraction of problems for which at least one of the NN particles is correct, in all twelve. In the internal-guidance ablations, it also increases surviving lineages and distinct outputs across both models and all reported benchmarks; on GSM8K with LLaDA-1.5, surviving lineages rise from 5.25.2 to 10.010.0 of 1616 (Table 2). How much of that coverage becomes final accuracy, however, depends on the selection rule.

Contributions.

(i) We formalize the mismatch between the ESS criterion and lineage diversity: multinomial resampling can eliminate distinct lineages while resetting the ESS to its maximum (Section 3). (ii) We address the two complementary sides of a resampling event: the weight floor bounds how far a lineage may collapse before the event, and Chopthin with carried weights bounds the ratio of the weights returned by it. We introduce both into block-wise masked diffusion SMC, derive the ESS lower bound implied by Chopthin’s ratio bound, tightening that of Gandy & Lau (2016) by a constant, and characterize the floor’s gate condition and bias (Section 4). (iii) We evaluate LP-SMC on four benchmarks and two base models, under internal guidance on all four benchmarks and under external process-reward guidance on the mathematics benchmarks, with a common reward-model selector for the headline comparison and a separate analysis of how coverage converts to accuracy under alternative selection rules (Section 5).

2 Background: particle decoding for masked diffusion LLMs

2.1 Masked diffusion decoding

Unlike autoregressive decoding, which extends a sequence from left to right, a diffusion LLM (Sahoo et al., 2024; Nie et al., 2025) starts from a fully masked sequence and replaces masked positions with tokens over a series of steps, several positions at a time (Appendix A collects the notation).

Setup.

A sequence has LL positions and tokens from a vocabulary 𝒱\mathcal{V}. Decoding runs backward over TT steps from the fully masked xTx_{T} to the output x0x_{0}. The positions are partitioned into consecutive blocks of fixed size; only positions of the current block can be committed, decoding moves on when the block is complete, and a particle whose block is complete waits until every particle has completed it. Resampling is considered at these boundaries.

One step.

With ℳt\mathcal{M}_{t} the masked positions of the current block, a step draws x^0(j)∼pθ(⋅∣xt)\hat{x}_{0}(j)\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{t}) at every j∈ℳtj\in\mathcal{M}_{t}, independently, at temperature one, where pθ(⋅∣xt)p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{t}) is the model’s predictive distribution given the partially masked sequence xtx_{t} (the prompt is implicit). It records the confidence ct​(j)=pθ​(x^0​(j)∣xt)c_{t}(j)=p_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{0}(j)\mid x_{t}). It commits the set 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t} of positions whose confidence exceeds a threshold (the most confident one if none does; ties by a fixed rule). It forms xt−1x_{t-1} by writing the drawn tokens at 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t} and copying everything else. Committed tokens are never revised.

2.2 Sequential Monte Carlo decoding

The sampler.

The sampler uses the decoder as its proposal and maintains NN particles; particle ii is a partially decoded sequence xt(i)x^{(i)}_{t} with weight Ut(i)U^{(i)}_{t} and either index is omitted when unambiguous. After the last block, a selection rule returns an answer from the final population; the rule is varied in Section 5.3. We write τ=(xT,…,x0)\tau=(x_{T},\dots,x_{0}) for a complete decoding path.

Kernel and potential.

For a step from xtx_{t} to xt−1x_{t-1}, the transition kernel Kt​(xt,xt−1)K_{t}(x_{t},x_{t-1}) is the probability that one decoding step moves xtx_{t} to xt−1x_{t-1}, including the token draws, the commit selection, and the copying of unmasked positions. The step also carries a potential Gt−1​(xt,xt−1)>0G_{t-1}(x_{t},x_{t-1})>0, a score of the tokens committed at that step. SR-SMC (Luo et al., 2026) takes the potential to be the product of the confidences of the committed tokens,

Gt−1​(xt,xt−1)=∏j∈𝒮tct​(j),G_{t-1}(x_{t},x_{t-1})=\prod_{j\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}c_{t}(j), (1)

so the decoder supplies its own incremental potential. Accumulated over steps this is the trajectory’s cumulative confidence, distinct from the per-step confidence that chooses the commit set. The potential need not be the decoder’s confidence: Section 5 also uses an external process reward model, and nothing below depends on where GG comes from.

Weights.

Between resampling events, the weight of a particle is built from the incremental weights of its steps:

Ut−1=Ut​Gt−1​(xt,xt−1),UT=1.U_{t-1}=U_{t}\,G_{t-1}(x_{t},x_{t-1}),\qquad U_{T}=1. (2)

This is the standard incremental weight of sequential Monte Carlo for the proposal qt−1=Ktq_{t-1}=K_{t} (Doucet et al., 2001), and it is the weight of SR-SMC. Weight degeneracy is monitored with the normalized weights wi=U(i)/∑kU(k)w_{i}=U^{(i)}/\sum_{k}U^{(k)} and the effective sample size ESS⁡(w)=1/∑iwi2∈[1,N]\mathrm{ESS}(w)=1/\sum_{i}w_{i}^{2}\in[1,N], evaluated at block boundaries; the sampler resamples when ESS<N/2\mathrm{ESS}<N/2, which we call the ESS gate.

What the weighted particles represent.

Let Q⁡(τ)Q(\tau) be the decoder path distribution and C⁡(τ)C(\tau) the accumulated potential, the product of the Gt−1G_{t-1} along the path. Without resampling, particles drawn from QQ and weighted by CC form a self-normalized importance-sampling approximation to the target with unnormalized density Q⁡(τ)​C​(τ)Q(\tau)\,C(\tau); a resampler that is unbiased in the sense of Section 2.3 preserves this weighted empirical measure in conditional expectation (Douc et al., 2005; Ahmadi et al., 2026), so changing the resampler changes the finite-particle representation of the target, not the target. The weight floor of Section 4.2, by contrast, explicitly modifies the measure, and Section 4.2 bounds the change.

2.3 Resampling operators

Every resampler in this paper takes the same input and returns the same kind of output. It receives the normalized weights w1:Nw_{1:N} and returns NN ancestors A1:NA_{1:N} and NN new weights w+1:Nw^{+}_{1:N}: output particle kk continues the state of input particle AkA_{k} and starts with weight wk+w^{+}_{k}. The number of offspring of input particle ii is Oi=|{k:Ak=i}|O_{i}=|\{k:A_{k}=i\}|; Oi=0O_{i}=0 means it has no descendants. We consider two existing resampling operators.

Multinomial.

The ancestors are drawn independently, Ak∼Categorical(w1:N)A_{k}\sim\mathrm{Categorical}(w_{1:N}) for k=1,…,Nk=1,\dots,N, and every returned weight is wk+=1/Nw^{+}_{k}=1/N, so particle ii receives Binomial⁡(N,wi)\mathrm{Binomial}(N,w_{i}) offspring; this is the resampler of SR-SMC. Stratified, residual and systematic schemes reduce the variance of the offspring counts but also return equal weights (Douc et al., 2005); Section 5.2 tests systematic resampling.

Chopthin.

Chopthin (Gandy & Lau, 2016) takes a ratio bound η≥4\eta\geq 4 and computes a threshold a>0a>0 from the weights. The expected number of offspring of particle ii is

haη(wi)={wi/a,wi<a(thin: kept with probability wi/a, weight set to a),1,a≤wi<ηa/2(keep: unchanged),2​wi/(η​a),wi≥ηa/2(chop: split into copies of equal weight),h^{\eta}_{a}(w_{i})=\begin{cases}w_{i}/a,&w_{i}<a\quad\text{(thin: kept with probability }w_{i}/a\text{, weight set to }a\text{)},\\ 1,&a\leq w_{i}<\eta a/2\quad\text{(keep: unchanged)},\\ 2w_{i}/(\eta a),&w_{i}\geq\eta a/2\quad\text{(chop: split into copies of equal weight)},\end{cases} (3)

where the threshold aa is chosen so that the expected offspring counts sum to NN; the coupled procedure returns exactly NN particles. Every returned weight lies in [a,η​a][a,\eta a], so the ratio of the largest to the smallest returned weight is at most η\eta, and the weights need not be equalized. Details of the integer allocation and the weight correction are given in Appendix B.1.

Multinomial resampling and Chopthin are both unbiased in the sense that the expected total offspring weight attributable to particle ii equals wiw_{i}, that is 𝔼[∑k:Ak=iwk+|w]=wi\mathbb{E}\big[\sum_{k:A_{k}=i}w^{+}_{k}\,\big|\,w\big]=w_{i} (Douc et al., 2005; Gandy & Lau, 2016), and therefore both preserve the target of Section 2.2. The rest of the paper varies two quantities: the resampling operator, and the weights it is given.

3 Motivation: what a resampling event discards

Under SR-SMC only 5.25.2 of 1616 lineages survive on GSM8K with LLaDA-1.5 and 1.11.1 with Dream-7B, and between 9.19.1 and 11.711.7 of 1616 particles lose all offspring per resampling event (Table 2, Section 5.2).

ESS and lineage diversity.

To count lineages, each particle carries a root r⁡(i)r(i): the index of the initial particle it descends from (two initial particles get different roots even if their sequences coincide). The number of surviving lineages RR is the number of distinct roots in the population. The ESS is a function of ww alone, and for every ww and every R∈{1,…,N}R\in\{1,\dots,N\} there is a root map with exactly RR distinct roots, so a trigger that depends only on the weights cannot tell how many lineages survive. Proposition 1 quantifies what it misses for the two resamplers of Section 2.3.

Proposition 1 (ESS-blindness).

Let 𝒫=(w,r)\mathcal{P}=(w,r) have positive weights, let 𝒫+=(w+,r+)\mathcal{P}^{+}=(w^{+},r^{+}) be the population after one resampling event applied to it, and let R+R^{+} be its number of lineages. For a root ρ\rho present in 𝒫\mathcal{P}, let wρ=∑i:r⁡(i)=ρwiw_{\rho}=\sum_{i:r(i)=\rho}w_{i} be the total weight of its lineage.

  1. (i)

    After multinomial resampling, ESS⁡(w+)=N\mathrm{ESS}(w^{+})=N always, while

    𝔼⁡[R+∣𝒫]=∑ρ(1−(1−wρ)N),\mathbb{E}[R^{+}\mid\mathcal{P}]=\sum_{\rho}\big(1-(1-w_{\rho})^{N}\big),

    the sum running over the RR roots present in 𝒫\mathcal{P}. For uniform weights and R=NR=N this is N⁡(1−(1−1/N)N)N\big(1-(1-1/N)^{N}\big): the expected surviving fraction 1−(1−1/N)N1-(1-1/N)^{N} decreases with NN to 1−e−1≈0.6321-e^{-1}\approx 0.632, and equals 0.6440.644 at N=16N=16, that is, 10.310.3 of 1616 lineages.

  2. (ii)

    If maxi⁡wi/mini⁡wi≤η/2\max_{i}w_{i}/\min_{i}w_{i}\leq\eta/2, then Chopthin returns 𝒫\mathcal{P} unchanged up to the order of the particles: every particle survives with its own weight, so w+=ww^{+}=w and R+=RR^{+}=R. Uniform weights always satisfy this condition.

The proof is in Appendix B.1.

Remark 1.

Parts (i) and (ii) describe two populations with the same weight statistics before and after the event (both start and end at ESS=N\mathrm{ESS}=N) whose genealogies differ by about a third of the lineages for any N≥4N\geq 4 (36%36\% at N=16N=16). The ESS does not distinguish them; a root count can. The loss in (i) is specific to multinomial resampling; on exactly uniform weights systematic or stratified resampling keeps every lineage (Douc et al., 2005), and Section 5.2 tests systematic resampling.

Requirements on the resampling operator.

Flattening the weights removes degeneracy at a cost at both ends of the weight distribution: a particle holding less than a 1/N1/N share is likely to receive no offspring, deleted on the basis of a weight that scores an unfinished prefix, while a heavy particle is copied into descendants that share a prefix, so an event never increases the number of distinct prefixes and usually decreases it (Doucet et al., 2001); Figure 1 shows both at one boundary. Neither cost is necessary: a resampling step need only leave the target unchanged, return NN particles and keep the weights from concentrating. Equalizing them is stronger than necessary: by Lemma 2 a bound of η\eta on the ratio of the largest to the smallest weight already implies ESS≥N/2\mathrm{ESS}\geq N/2, and Chopthin enforces exactly this bound on the weights it returns (Section 4.1). That bound constrains only the output of the step; a particle whose weight is far below the maximum when the resampler is called is removed with probability approaching one under any such rule, and the weight floor bounds this input-side gap (Section 4.2). Neither bound depends on the origin of the weights, so both apply when the potential is a reward model.

4 LP-SMC: Chopthin resampling with a weight floor

LP-SMC denotes the population-management step only: Chopthin resampling with the weight floor of Section 4.2. The guidance signal and the selection rule are varied separately in Section 5.

At a block boundary.

(i) the running weights UU have been updated by equation 2 through the block; (ii) the floor of Section 4.2 is applied, giving U~\tilde{U} and w~\tilde{w}; (iii) if ESS⁡(w~)<N/2\mathrm{ESS}(\tilde{w})<N/2, Chopthin (Section 4.1) is applied to w~\tilde{w} and each particle continues from its ancestor with weight w+w^{+}; (iv) otherwise every particle continues with weight U~\tilde{U}. Decoding then resumes.

4.1 Chopthin resampling in diffusion SMC

We modify diffusion SMC only at the population-management stage. The decoder transition KtK_{t}, the potential Gt−1G_{t-1}, the block schedule and the ESS<N/2\mathrm{ESS}<N/2 trigger are unchanged and no model evaluations are added. The population-management step therefore applies whether the boundary weights come from accumulated decoder confidence or an external reward model. We replace the resampling step by Chopthin (Gandy & Lau, 2016) with carried weights (Ahmadi et al., 2026):

(A1:N,w1:N+)=Chopthin(w1:N,η),x(k)←x(Ak),U(k)←wk+.(A_{1:N},w^{+}_{1:N})=\mathrm{Chopthin}(w_{1:N},\eta),\qquad x^{(k)}\leftarrow x^{(A_{k})},\qquad U^{(k)}\leftarrow w^{+}_{k}. (4)

The assignments are simultaneous: output particle kk continues the full state of input particle AkA_{k}, including its root label and cached decoder state. The returned weights are defined up to a common factor; under internal guidance they are carried into the next block instead of being reset; under external guidance the weight is rebuilt from the reward model at each boundary (Section 5, Setup). Since every returned weight lies in [a,η​a][a,\eta a], Lemma 2 gives ESS⁡(w+)≥4​η​N/(η+1)2\mathrm{ESS}(w^{+})\geq 4\eta N/(\eta+1)^{2}, which tightens the bound of Gandy & Lau (2016) by a constant. We use η=3+8\eta=3+\sqrt{8} throughout, for which the bound is exactly N/2N/2: an event cannot leave the population below the threshold that triggered it. This is a guarantee on the weights, not on the number of lineages. The quantities have separate roles: the potential sets how far the weights spread, η\eta sets the spread of the resampler’s output, the floor of Section 4.2 sets how much it tolerates on its input, and the ESS gate sets when the resampler is called at all.

4.2 Flooring the input weights

Chopthin bounds the ratio of the weights it returns, not of the weights it is given, and a particle whose weight is far below the maximum is removed with high probability regardless of the output bound. We therefore bound the input ratio as well. At a block boundary let Umax=maxk⁡U(k)U_{\max}=\max_{k}U^{(k)}; the floored weights are

U~(i)=max⁡(U(i),e−κ​Umax),w~i=U~(i)/∑jU~(j),κ>0.\tilde{U}^{(i)}=\max\!\big(U^{(i)},\,e^{-\kappa}U_{\max}\big),\quad\tilde{w}_{i}=\tilde{U}^{(i)}\Big/\sum_{j}\tilde{U}^{(j)},\quad\kappa>0. (5)

The gate tests ESS⁡(w~)<N/2\mathrm{ESS}(\tilde{w})<N/2 and the resampler receives w~\tilde{w}. The floor is a deterministic map that needs no model evaluation and applies to any resampler; it leaves the maximum unchanged and raises the lowest weights, the opposite end of the distribution from Chopthin’s chop step.

Under internal guidance the floored or post-resampling weights are carried forward: between boundaries Ut−1=U~t​Gt−1U_{t-1}=\tilde{U}_{t}\,G_{t-1}, with the floor re-applied at every boundary. Under external guidance weights are rebuilt at every boundary, so neither the floor-induced increase nor the returned Chopthin weights persist; this is a boundary-wise reweighting, not the accumulated potential of equation 2, so we treat the externally guided setting as a robustness check and not as the same Feynman–Kac target (Del Moral, 2004).

After equation 5 the ratio of U~\tilde{U} is at most eκe^{\kappa}, so Lemma 2 applies to the weights that the gate and the resampler receive: ESS≥4​eκ​N/(eκ+1)2\mathrm{ESS}\geq 4e^{\kappa}N/(e^{\kappa}+1)^{2}. The ESS gate imposes a lower bound on κ\kappa; we then choose κ=ln⁡N\kappa=\ln N to keep the floor non-vacuous.

Gate compatibility. Once this lower bound exceeds the gate threshold, resampling is never triggered; the sampler resamples only when

κ>κ⋆:=ln⁡(3+8)≈1.763.\kappa\;>\;\kappa^{\star}:=\ln\big(3+\sqrt{8}\big)\approx 1.763. (6)

The corresponding ratio eκ⋆=3+8e^{\kappa^{\star}}=3+\sqrt{8} equals the Chopthin ratio bound η\eta of Section 4.1; both are chosen so that the worst admissible weight profile has ESS=N/2\mathrm{ESS}=N/2.

Choice of κ\kappa. Conversely, as κ\kappa grows the bound falls back to zero and the floor has no effect. We use κ=ln⁡N\kappa=\ln N, a floor at 1/N1/N of the maximum weight, which satisfies the gate condition for N≥6N\geq 6 (at N=16N=16, κ=2.77\kappa=2.77 against κ⋆=1.76\kappa^{\star}=1.76). Under this floor a particle’s normalized weight is at least 1/(N⁡(N−1)+1)1/(N(N-1)+1), so a multinomial ancestor draw keeps it with probability at least 1−(1−1/(N⁡(N−1)+1))N1-(1-1/(N(N-1)+1))^{N}, 0.0640.064 at N=16N=16 (Appendix B.3); without the floor no positive lower bound exists. Empirically, in the GSM8K lineage-risk analysis, no correctly answered problem under either floored LP-SMC configuration reaches the corresponding deletion probability of 0.9360.936 (Table 8, Appendix D).

Raising low weights changes what the resampler is unbiased for. Resampling remains unbiased, but for the floored weights w~\tilde{w} rather than the original ww. The change is confined to the particles the floor actually touches: a particle already within κ\kappa nats of the maximum keeps its weight exactly, and only particles below that threshold are raised, to e−κe^{-\kappa} of the maximum. Under internal guidance the raised value persists until the next resampling event.

The size of the change is bounded. At a single boundary the floor can shift at most (N−1)/(2​N−1)(N-1)/(2N-1) of the normalized mass onto floored particles, which is 0.480.48 at N=16N=16, and that worst case arises only when N−1N-1 of the NN particles sit on the floor at once. In the measured runs the mass on floored particles is about an order of magnitude smaller (Appendix B.3). The floor is therefore an explicit and bounded change to the weights, in the same family as the weight flattening used by particle methods for reasoning (Giannone et al., 2025).

5 Experiments

Setup.

The decoders are LLaDA-1.5 (Nie et al., 2025) and Dream-7B (Ye et al., 2025). Both run with generation length L=256L=256, block size 3232, eight decoding steps per block, confidence-threshold commitment at 0.90.9, temperature 1.01.0 and N=16N=16 particles. Resampling is gated at ESS<N/2\mathrm{ESS}<N/2; Chopthin uses η=3+8\eta=3+\sqrt{8} and the floor κ=ln⁡N\kappa=\ln N. Under internal guidance the weight accumulates by equation 2; under external guidance it is rebuilt at every boundary from the log-odds of the mean step score of Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B (Yang et al., 2024) on the current prefix, as in Puri et al. (2025) (Appendix B.5 gives the exact definition). Benchmarks are MATH-500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2024) (4-shot), GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) (5-shot), HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021) (0-shot) and MBPP (Austin et al., 2021) (3-shot), on the full test set of each; grading and shot conventions are in Appendix B.6. The population-management operations introduce no direct decoder or reward-model evaluations; Appendix B.6 reports measured end-to-end NFE and wall time.

5.1 Main comparison

Table 1 is the primary controlled comparison. Within each pair the model, the guidance signal, the selection rule and the problems are held fixed and only the population step changes, multinomial resampling against LP-SMC, so a difference between the two rows cannot arise from the selection rule. LP-SMC has the higher accuracy in eleven of the twelve accuracy cells, under the decoder’s confidence on all four benchmarks for both models and under the external reward model on the mathematics benchmarks for LLaDA-1.5; the exception is Dream-7B on MATH-500 under external guidance, 49.249.2 against 48.248.2. Coverage is higher under LP-SMC in all twelve settings (Figure 2), and the coverage gains are also the better supported: of the 95%95\% bootstrap intervals on the paired differences (Appendix E), six of the twelve accuracy intervals include zero and eleven of the twelve coverage intervals exclude it, and none favours the baseline.
